title: 05 — Creating Data
html:
05 — Creating Data

The one idea: state the schema, parse strictly, and seed every random number. Data you create, whether two hand-written rows or a million synthetic trades, should be exactly what you meant and identical on every run.

1. What it is

Source How
Python dicts or records pl.DataFrame(records), then strict cast to the types you want
Columns pl.DataFrame({"a": [...], "b": [...]})
NumPy Pass arrays as columns (zero-copy for numeric types where possible)
Ranges and sequences pl.int_range, pl.date_range, pl.datetime_range
Random data NumPy default_rng(seed), or Series.sample(..., seed=...)
Nested values Aggregate into list, build with pl.struct
Existing frames pl.from_pandas, pl.from_arrow, pl.from_numpy

2. Why it matters

  • Tests need small, exact fixtures. Benchmarks and load tests need large, realistic, repeatable data.
  • Schema inference guesses from the first values it sees. One odd value can turn a whole column into strings, or into nulls.
  • Unseeded randomness makes failures impossible to reproduce.

3. The main ideas

3.1 Parse strictly

cast is strict by default: a value that can't convert raises InvalidOperationError and names it. Some paths are not strict and quietly produce nulls:

  • schema_overrides applied to text in the DataFrame constructor;
  • str.to_decimal, and cast(..., strict=False).

After any parse, check null_count() on columns that must be complete.

3.2 Realistic shapes

Real data isn't uniform. Amounts are skewed (lognormal), sides and categories have weights, and dates cluster. Building those shapes into synthetic data makes performance tests honest, for example group sizes and join fan-out.

3.3 Joins for reference data

Generate a small dimension (funds, accounts) and join it on, rather than generating every attribute per row. This mirrors how real data is shaped, and keeps foreign keys valid.

4. Working code

The script shows the silent-null trap and the strict fix, generates one million seeded trades with a fund dimension, builds nested columns, and checks the schema survives a Parquet round trip.

from datetime import date
import numpy as np
import polars as pl

pl.Config.set_tbl_rows(6)

# 1. From Python data. Parse with a strict cast: a bad value should fail loudly, not become null.
records = [
    {"scheme_code": "SCH001", "nav_date": date(2026, 11, 2), "nav": "101.2345", "units": 1_500},
    {"scheme_code": "SCH002", "nav_date": date(2026, 11, 2), "nav": "54.1000", "units": 820},
]
trap = pl.DataFrame(records, schema_overrides={"nav": pl.Decimal(12, 4)})
print("schema_overrides on text gave nulls:", trap["nav"].null_count(), "of", trap.height)
small = pl.DataFrame(records).with_columns(pl.col("nav").cast(pl.Decimal(12, 4)))   # strict by default
print(small)
try:
    pl.DataFrame({"nav": ["12.5", "n/a"]}).with_columns(pl.col("nav").cast(pl.Decimal(12, 4)))
except pl.exceptions.InvalidOperationError as err:
    print("strict cast refused:", str(err).splitlines()[0])
print()

# 2. Synthetic test data at scale: generate with expressions, seed the randomness, keep it reproducible.
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)
n = 1_000_000
funds = pl.DataFrame({"fund_id": range(1, 51),
                      "category": ["EQUITY", "DEBT", "HYBRID", "INDEX", "LIQUID"] * 10})
trades = (
    pl.DataFrame({
        "trade_id": pl.int_range(1, n + 1, eager=True),
        "fund_id": rng.integers(1, 51, n),
        "amount": rng.lognormal(mean=9, sigma=1.2, size=n).round(2),
        "side": rng.choice(["BUY", "SELL"], size=n, p=[0.6, 0.4]),
    })
    .with_columns(
        pl.date_range(date(2026, 1, 1), date(2026, 12, 31), "1d", eager=True)
          .sample(n, with_replacement=True, seed=7).alias("trade_date"),
        pl.col("side").cast(pl.Enum(["BUY", "SELL"])),
    )
    .join(funds, on="fund_id", how="left", maintain_order="left")
    .with_columns(pl.col("category").cast(pl.Categorical))
)
print(trades.head(3))
print("rows:", trades.height, "| size:", round(trades.estimated_size("mb"), 1), "MB")
print(trades.group_by("category").agg(pl.len(), pl.col("amount").sum().cast(pl.Int64)).sort("category"))

# 3. Nested data: lists and structs build naturally from aggregations.
basket = trades.head(1000).group_by("fund_id").agg(
    pl.col("amount").top_k(3).alias("top3"),
    pl.struct(pl.col("amount").min().alias("lo"), pl.col("amount").max().alias("hi")).alias("range"),
).sort("fund_id").head(2)
print(basket)

# 4. Write it once in a columnar format; read it back with the schema intact.
trades.write_parquet("data/trades.parquet")
print("round-trip schema equal:", pl.read_parquet_schema("data/trades.parquet") == trades.schema)

What to notice:

  • schema_overrides on text produced 2 nulls out of 2, with no error. The strict cast parsed the same text correctly, and refused "n/a" with a message that names the value.
  • Seeds make the whole frame reproducible. Rerun it and the first trades, totals and top-3 lists are identical.
  • Enum for side and Categorical for category keep the million rows at 31.5 MB.
  • The Parquet round trip kept every type, including Enum and Categorical. CSV would not.

5. Common mistakes

  1. Relying on schema inference for anything that matters (IDs with leading zeros, decimals, dates).
  2. strict=False or overrides that swallow bad values without a null check afterwards.
  3. Unseeded random data in tests.
  4. Uniform synthetic data that hides skew problems real data has.
  5. Saving test data as CSV, losing types, then re-inferring them wrongly.

6. Exercise (45 minutes)

  1. Add a settlement_date two business days after trade_date (look at dt.add_business_days).
  2. Make 1% of amounts null and 0.1% negative, then write a check that finds both.
  3. Generate 50 million rows with a lazy plan and sink_parquet, and compare peak memory with building it eagerly.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why can schema_overrides be dangerous on text input?
  2. How do you make synthetic data reproducible?
  3. Why generate a dimension table and join it, rather than generating every column per row?
  4. Which file format keeps Enum and Decimal types intact?
  5. What should you check after any non-strict parse?

Answers

  1. Values that don't parse become null without an error.
  2. Seed every random generator (default_rng(seed), sample(seed=...)).
  3. It matches how real data is shaped, keeps keys consistent, and is cheaper to generate.
  4. Parquet (and Arrow IPC).
  5. null_count() on every column that must be complete.
